content: Mees' lines, also known as Aldrich-Mees' lines, are transverse bands of discoloration that appear across the nails of the fingers and toes. These lines are typically white in color and are associated with episodes of poisoning, particularly with arsenic, thallium, or other heavy metals. As the nail grows, these lines gradually move distally toward the free edge of the nail and eventually disappear when the affected portion of the nail is trimmed. The phenomenon was first described by A.S.J. Aldrich in 1901 and 1904. From a pathophysiological perspective, Mees' lines are linked to systemic conditions or toxic exposures. They are most commonly associated with poisoning by arsenic, thallium, or other heavy metals. Renal failure has also been implicated as a potential cause. In rare cases, Mees' lines may be observed in individuals with fluorosis or leprosy. Diagnosis of Mees' lines is primarily clinical and involves physical examination of the nails. The characteristic white bands traversing the width of the nail are a key diagnostic feature.
